subject: system-design
question: What is the core challenge of a transaction that spans multiple shards?
options: Each shard requires a different SQL dialect
Shards are not allowed to store more than one table
Coordinating an atomic commit across shards, typically with 2PC or saga-style compensation
Transactions are disabled by default on every shard
explanation: Atomicity across independent databases needs a coordination protocol, which adds latency and failure modes.

subject: system-design
question: What is the main tradeoff of hash-based sharding compared with range-based sharding?
options: Range queries become faster while writes concentrate on one shard
Keys spread evenly, but range scans must query many shards
Adding shards never requires moving any data
Joins become local to a single shard automatically
explanation: Hashing destroys key ordering, so range queries touch many shards, while range sharding risks hotspots.

subject: system-design
question: Why is random jitter added to retry delays?
options: It guarantees that retries succeed on the first attempt
It reduces the number of TCP packets sent
It forces requests to arrive in strict FIFO order
It spreads retries out so many clients do not hit a recovering service at the same moment
explanation: Synchronized retries create spikes that can prevent a recovering service from catching up.

subject: system-design
question: Why does consistent hashing reduce data movement compared with hash(key) mod N?
options: It guarantees strict global ordering of keys across nodes
Adding or removing a node remaps only a small fraction of keys instead of nearly all of them
It places every key on every node
It eliminates the need for replication
explanation: With mod N, changing N reshuffles most keys; on a hash ring only keys adjacent to the changed node move.

subject: system-design
question: Which is an example of graceful degradation?
options: Returning HTTP 500 for every request when any dependency fails
Showing a product page without personalized recommendations when the recommendation service is down
Disabling checkout whenever a cache miss occurs
Turning off all logging when a dependency is slow
explanation: The core experience keeps working while a non-critical feature is reduced or removed.

subject: system-design
question: Which approach avoids explicit invalidation when content changes?
options: Lowering the TTL to one millisecond for every key
Disabling the cache during every write
Storing each entry twice on the same cache node
Embedding a content version or hash in the cache key so changed content gets a new key
explanation: Old keys simply stop being requested and age out, so no delete is needed.

subject: system-design
question: In a write-through cache, when is a write acknowledged to the client?
options: After it has been written to both the cache and the backing store
After it is written only to the cache, before the store is updated
Only after the entry is evicted from the cache
After the next read of the same key
explanation: Write-through trades higher write latency for the guarantee that the cache and store agree.

subject: system-design
question: Which response best tells a client to back off and retry later?
options: 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header
401 Unauthorized with a WWW-Authenticate header
404 Not Found with a Location header
400 Bad Request with a Retry-After header
explanation: 429 signals rate limiting, and Retry-After indicates how long to wait before retrying.

subject: system-design
question: A user saves a profile change, then immediately reads from a replica and sees the old value. What anomaly is this?
options: Split brain
Write skew
A read-your-writes violation caused by replication lag
Cache penetration
explanation: The primary acknowledged the write, but the lagging replica has not yet applied it.

subject: system-design
question: Where does Kafka guarantee ordering of records?
options: Within a single partition
Across all topics in the cluster
Across all partitions of a topic
Across every consumer group independently
explanation: Ordering is per partition; there is no global order across partitions.
